# Statistical Inference {#sec-intro-inference .unnumbered}

Statistical inference is the branch of statistics dedicated to distinguishing patterns arising from signal versus those arising from chance. When a usability study finds that 48% of participants rate a new interface positively, or an experiment finds that responses are 40 ms slower in one condition than in another, inference tells us how much these numbers could change if we ran the study again, and whether a difference is large enough not to be explained by chance alone.

In this part of the book, we show how the probability concepts from the previous part can be applied to develop these methods. To illustrate the concepts, we supplement mathematical formulas with Monte Carlo simulations and R code.

We begin with estimates, standard errors, margins of error and confidence intervals, using a satisfaction survey as the running example (@sec-estimates-and-ci). We then introduce hypothesis testing, p-values and statistical power, starting from a participant who may or may not be guessing in a two-choice task (@sec-hypothesis-testing). Finally, we compare two groups or two conditions, the most common question in behavioural research, with the t-test and the Wilcoxon test (@sec-two-groups).

:::{.callout-note}
Irizarry's original book develops inference through a case study on election forecasting, including chapters on data-driven models, Bayesian statistics, hierarchical models and the bootstrap. These chapters are not part of this edition yet: the estimates and hypothesis-testing chapters have been rewritten around behavioural examples, and the chapter on comparing two groups is new.
:::
